title: Probability
tagline: Experimental and theoretical probability, sample space, events, and simple compound probability problems.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Mathematics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every numerical result in this chapter was independently recomputed. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Probability is the study of the likelihood of events occurring. In ICSE Class X, the focus is on theoretical (classical) probability, where all outcomes are equally likely. The chapter covers the definition of probability as the ratio of favourable outcomes to total equally likely outcomes, the sample space (the set of all possible outcomes), and events (subsets of the sample space). Students learn to calculate probabilities for single experiments (coin toss, die throw, card draw) and simple compound events involving 'and' (intersection) and 'or' (union). The chapter also covers the complementary event: P(not E) = 1 − P(E).

learningOutcomes: Define the sample space of a random experiment and identify the total number of equally likely outcomes.
Calculate the probability of a single event: P(E) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes.
Calculate the probability of the complementary event: P(not E) = 1 − P(E).
Calculate the probability of simple compound events: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B), and P(A and B) for independent events.
Solve probability problems involving coins, dice, cards, and everyday objects.
Distinguish between independent and dependent events (basic understanding).
Express probability as a fraction, decimal, or percentage, and interpret the result.

blocks.text: Probability measures the likelihood that an event will occur. It is expressed as a number between 0 and 1, where 0 means the event is impossible and 1 means the event is certain (sure). The theoretical (classical) definition of probability, which is used in ICSE Class X, assumes that all outcomes of an experiment are equally likely. The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes. An event is a subset of the sample space — one or more outcomes that we are interested in. The probability of an event E is given by P(E) = (number of outcomes favourable to E) / (total number of equally likely outcomes). The complementary event 'not E' has probability P(not E) = 1 − P(E).

A convenient way to picture an experiment is to list its sample space: for a single coin toss the space is {H, T}, and for two tosses it is {HH, HT, TH, TT}. Events are selections from the space — for example, 'at least one head' collects HH, HT and TH. A Venn diagram draws the same information, with each event enclosed as a region inside the sample-space boundary.

items: Probability is a number between 0 and 1 (inclusive).
P(E) = 1 means the event is certain; P(E) = 0 means the event is impossible.
The complementary event satisfies P(not E) = 1 − P(E).
Theoretical probability assumes all outcomes are equally likely.
The sample space lists all possible outcomes.

learn.title: Sample Space
learn.Title: Sample Space and Equally Likely Outcomes

blocks.text: The sample space of a random experiment is the set of all possible outcomes. In ICSE Class X, the most common experiments are: (a) tossing a fair coin, with sample space {H, T}; (b) throwing a fair die, with sample space {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}; (c) drawing a card from a well-shuffled deck of 52 playing cards, with 4 suits (spades, hearts, diamonds, clubs) and 13 ranks (A, 2, 3, …, 10, J, Q, K) in each suit. Two events are equally likely if they have the same probability of occurring. For a fair coin or fair die, all outcomes in the sample space are equally likely.

items.text: Write the sample space for tossing a coin twice.
items.answer: Sample space = {HH, HT, TH, TT}. There are 4 equally likely outcomes.
items.explanation: The first toss can be H or T, and the second toss can be H or T, giving 2 × 2 = 4 outcomes.

items.text: Write the sample space for throwing a die and getting a number less than 4.
items.answer: Sample space = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. The event 'number less than 4' = {1, 2, 3}. P(number < 4) = 3/6 = 1/2.
items.explanation: The die has 6 faces, all equally likely. Three outcomes (1, 2, 3) are less than 4.

items.text: Write the sample space for drawing a card from a standard deck and getting a queen.
items.answer: Sample space = 52 cards. The event 'queen' = 4 outcomes (queen of spades, hearts, diamonds, clubs). P(queen) = 4/52 = 1/13.
items.explanation: A standard deck has 52 cards, 4 of which are queens.

items: The sample space for a coin toss is {H, T}; for a die throw, {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
For multiple coins/dice, the sample space is the Cartesian product: e.g., two coins give {HH, HT, TH, TT}.
All outcomes in a sample space for a fair experiment are equally likely.
The total number of outcomes for drawing a card from a 52-card deck is 52.

blocks.text: The probability of an event E is P(E) = n(E) / n(S), where n(E) is the number of outcomes favourable to E, and n(S) is the total number of outcomes in the sample space S. The probability of the complementary event 'not E' is P(not E) = 1 − P(E). A sure event has probability 1; an impossible event has probability 0. For any event E, 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1.

items.text: A die is thrown. Find the probability of getting (i) a number greater than 4, (ii) an even number, (iii) a number less than 7.
items.answer: (i) P(number > 4) = 2/6 = 1/3 (favourable outcomes: 5, 6). (ii) P(even number) = 3/6 = 1/2 (favourable outcomes: 2, 4, 6). (iii) P(number < 7) = 6/6 = 1 (sure event; all outcomes are less than 7).
items.explanation: The sample space has 6 equally likely outcomes. (i) Two outcomes (5, 6) are greater than 4. (ii) Three outcomes (2, 4, 6) are even. (iii) All six outcomes are less than 7.

items.text: A card is drawn from a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards. Find the probability of drawing (i) a king, (ii) a red card, (iii) a king or a red card.
items.answer: (i) P(king) = 4/52 = 1/13. (ii) P(red card) = 26/52 = 1/2. (iii) P(king or red) = P(king) + P(red) − P(king and red) = 4/52 + 26/52 − 2/52 = 28/52 = 7/13. (There are 2 red kings.)
items.explanation: Use the addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). There are 4 kings and 26 red cards, but 2 cards are both kings and red (king of hearts and king of diamonds).

items.text: A bag contains 5 red balls, 3 blue balls, and 2 green balls. A ball is drawn at random. Find the probability that the ball is (i) red, (ii) not red, (iii) blue or green.
items.explanation: Total balls = 10. (i) 5 are red. (ii) The complementary event 'not red' has probability 1 − 1/2 = 1/2. (iii) 3 blue + 2 green = 5 favourable outcomes out of 10.

items: P(E) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes.
P(not E) = 1 − P(E).
P(E) = 1 is a sure event; P(E) = 0 is an impossible event.
For compound events, use P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
Probability is always between 0 and 1 inclusive.

blocks.text: For two events A and B: (a) P(A and B) is the probability that both A and B occur. If A and B are independent (the occurrence of one does not affect the other), then P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). (b) P(A or B) is the probability that at least one of A or B occurs. The general rule is P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). This accounts for the overlap where both A and B occur (otherwise they would be counted twice).

items.text: A die is thrown twice. Find the probability of getting a 6 on the first throw and a 5 on the second throw.
items.answer: P(6 on first and 5 on second) = P(6 on first) × P(5 on second) = (1/6) × (1/6) = 1/36.
items.explanation: The two throws are independent events. The outcome of the first does not affect the second. P(6 on first) = 1/6, P(5 on second) = 1/6, so P(both) = 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36.

items.text: A die is thrown. Find the probability of getting a number that is either a 3 or an even number.
items.answer: P(3 or even) = P(3) + P(even) − P(3 and even). P(3) = 1/6, P(even) = 3/6, P(3 and even) = 0 (3 is not even). So P(3 or even) = 1/6 + 3/6 − 0 = 4/6 = 2/3.
items.explanation: The events 'getting a 3' and 'getting an even number' are mutually exclusive (they cannot happen simultaneously), so P(3 and even) = 0, and the addition rule simplifies to P(A) + P(B).

items.text: A bag contains 3 red balls and 2 blue balls. Two balls are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability that both are red.
items.answer: P(first red and second red) = (3/5) × (2/4) = 6/20 = 3/10. (After drawing a red ball, there are 2 red out of 4 remaining.)
items.explanation: The draws are without replacement, so the second probability depends on the first. P(first red) = 3/5. Given first red, P(second red) = 2/4 = 1/2. Multiply: 3/5 × 1/2 = 3/10.

items: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) for independent events.
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B) (general addition rule).
If A and B are mutually exclusive (cannot both happen), then P(A and B) = 0 and P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
Without replacement: probabilities change after each draw; with replacement: probabilities stay the same.
Always check whether events are independent, mutually exclusive, or neither.

blocks.text: The complement of an event E, denoted 'not E' or E', is the event that E does not occur. The key relationship is P(not E) = 1 − P(E). This is useful when it is easier to calculate the probability that an event does not happen than that it does. For example, 'at least one' problems are often solved by computing P(none) = 1 − P(none of the desired outcomes).

items.text: A die is thrown. Find the probability of getting at least one 6 in two throws.
items.answer: P(at least one 6) = 1 − P(no 6 in two throws) = 1 − (5/6)² = 1 − 25/36 = 11/36.
items.explanation: It is easier to compute the probability of the complementary event 'no 6 in two throws'. P(no 6 on one throw) = 5/6. For two independent throws: (5/6)² = 25/36. Then P(at least one 6) = 1 − 25/36 = 11/36.

items.text: A box contains 5 defective and 10 non-defective bulbs. Two bulbs are drawn at random. Find the probability that at least one is defective.
items.answer: P(at least one defective) = 1 − P(both non-defective) = 1 − (10/15) × (9/14) = 1 − 90/210 = 1 − 3/7 = 4/7.
items.explanation: P(first non-defective) = 10/15 = 2/3. Given first non-defective, P(second non-defective) = 9/14. So P(both non-defective) = (2/3) × (9/14) = 18/42 = 3/7. Then P(at least one defective) = 1 − 3/7 = 4/7.

items.text: A factory produces light bulbs. 2% of the bulbs are defective. If a quality inspector randomly selects 3 bulbs, find the probability that at least one is defective.
items.answer: P(at least one defective) = 1 − P(none defective) = 1 − (0.98)³ = 1 − 0.941192 = 0.058808 ≈ 5.88%.
items.explanation: P(none defective) = (0.98)³ because the probability of a non-defective bulb is 0.98, and the selections are independent (with replacement or from a large population). P(at least one defective) = 1 − 0.941192 = 0.058808.

items: P(not E) = 1 − P(E) is the key complementary relationship.
Complementary events are useful for 'at least one' problems: compute P(none) and subtract from 1.
If events are drawn without replacement, the probabilities change; if with replacement, they stay the same.
The complementary event 'not E' includes all outcomes in the sample space that are not in E.

blocks.text: This section summarises the sample spaces and probabilities for the standard experiments used in ICSE Class X: coin tosses, die throws, and card draws. Students should be able to quickly write the sample space and compute probabilities for any event within it.

blocks.caption: Standard experiments: sample spaces and probabilities

items: Coin: 2 outcomes; two coins: 4 outcomes; three coins: 8 outcomes (2ⁿ).
Die: 6 outcomes; two dice: 36 outcomes (6²).
Card deck: 52 outcomes; jokerless.
Memorise these sample spaces; they are used in most probability problems.
For 'at least one' problems, use the complementary: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).

blocks.text: The questions that follow move from defining sample spaces and computing basic probabilities through compound events and complementary events to standard experiment problems. Work each one by identifying the experiment, writing the sample space, and applying the probability formula.

figures.caption: Figure: The probability scale
figures.description: Every probability lies on the scale from 0 (an impossible event) to 1 (a certain event); a value of 1/2 means the event is as likely to happen as not.

figures.caption: Figure: Sample-space tree diagram for two experiments
figures.description: A tree diagram lists every outcome of a multi-stage experiment, for example a coin toss followed by a die throw: 2 × 6 = 12 equally likely outcomes, each branch carrying its probability.

keyPoints: P(E) = n(E) ÷ n(S) holds only when every outcome in the sample space S is equally likely.
Every probability satisfies 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1: P(certain event) = 1 and P(impossible event) = 0.
P(not E) = 1 − P(E) — use the complement whenever “at least one” makes direct counting tedious.
For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
For any two events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); the subtraction removes the double-counted overlap.
A pack of 52 cards has 4 suits of 13 cards, 13 hearts, 4 kings, and exactly one card that is both a king and a heart.
A fair die has sample space {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} and a fair coin {H, T}; list the space explicitly when asked.
A probability such as 29/52 that does not simplify is left as it is — never force a simplification.
examFocus: Card questions test the addition rule through king/heart overlaps — always subtract the intersection that is counted twice.
“At least one” wording signals the complement: compute 1 − P(none) instead of adding many cases.
Two-dice questions have 36 equally likely outcomes; count the favourable pairs rather than multiplying face probabilities blindly.
Writing the sample space earns separate marks from the final probability — show it in full.

vocabulary.meaning: The set of all possible equally likely outcomes of an experiment.
A subset of the sample space: a selection of outcomes to which a probability is assigned.
An outcome that satisfies the event in question.
The event that E does not occur; its probability is 1 − P(E).
Events for which the outcome of one does not change the probability of the other.
An event that must occur; its probability is 1.
An event that cannot occur; its probability is 0.

questions.prompt: A coin is tossed. The probability of getting a head is _____.
questions.explanation: The sample space is {H, T}, with 2 equally likely outcomes. The favourable outcome is H, so P(head) = 1/2.

questions.prompt: A die is thrown. The probability of getting a number greater than 6 is _____.
questions.explanation: A standard die has faces {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}; no outcome is greater than 6, so the event is impossible and P = 0.

questions.prompt: A die is thrown. The probability of getting an even number is _____.
questions.explanation: The even numbers are {2, 4, 6}, so 3 favourable outcomes out of 6: P = 3/6 = 1/2.

questions.prompt: Two coins are tossed simultaneously. Find the probability of getting (i) exactly one head, (ii) at most one head.
questions.answer: (i) P(exactly one head) = 2/4 = 1/2 (favourable outcomes: HT, TH). (ii) P(at most one head) = 3/4 (favourable outcomes: HH, HT, TH; only TT has two heads).
questions.explanation: The sample space for two coins is {HH, HT, TH, TT}. (i) Exactly one head: HT and TH, so 2/4 = 1/2. (ii) At most one head: HH, HT, TH (three outcomes), so 3/4.

questions.prompt: A card is drawn from a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards. Find the probability of drawing a king or a queen.
questions.answer: P(king or queen) = 4/52 + 4/52 = 8/52 = 2/13. (Kings and queens are mutually exclusive.)
questions.explanation: There are 4 kings and 4 queens in a 52-card deck. Since a card cannot be both a king and a queen, the events are mutually exclusive, and P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

questions.prompt: A bag contains 4 white, 5 black, and 3 red balls. A ball is drawn at random. Find the probability that the ball is white or red.
questions.explanation: Total balls = 12. There are 4 white and 3 red, so 7 favourable outcomes. Since a ball cannot be both white and red, the events are mutually exclusive: P = 7/12.

questions.prompt: A die is thrown twice. Find the probability of getting a 5 at least once.
questions.answer: P(at least one 5) = 1 − P(no 5 in two throws) = 1 − (5/6)² = 1 − 25/36 = 11/36.
questions.explanation: The complementary event 'no 5 in two throws' has probability (5/6) × (5/6) = 25/36. So P(at least one 5) = 1 − 25/36 = 11/36.

questions.prompt: From a pack of 52 cards, a card is drawn at random. Find the probability that the card is (i) a king, (ii) a heart, (iii) a king and a heart, (iv) a king or a heart.
questions.answer: (i) 4/52 = 1/13. (ii) 26/52 = 1/2. (iii) 1/52 — only the king of hearts is both a king and a heart. (iv) 29/52 — by the addition rule, P(king or heart) = 4/52 + 26/52 − 1/52 = 29/52.
questions.explanation: (i) 4 kings out of 52 cards. (ii) 13 hearts out of 52 cards. (iii) Only the king of hearts is both a king and a heart, so 1/52. (iv) Using the addition rule: P(king or heart) = P(king) + P(heart) − P(king and heart) = 4/52 + 26/52 − 1/52 = 29/52.

questions.prompt: A box contains 3 defective and 7 non-defective bulbs. Two bulbs are drawn at random. Find the probability that both are non-defective.
questions.explanation: P(first non-defective) = 7/10. Given first non-defective, there are 6 non-defective out of 9 remaining, so P(second non-defective) = 6/9 = 2/3. Multiply: 7/10 × 2/3 = 14/30 = 7/15.

questions.prompt: A bag contains 5 white, 7 red, and 3 black balls. Two balls are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability that (i) both are red, (ii) one is white and one is red, (iii) at least one is black.
questions.explanation: (i) P(first red) = 7/15. Given first red, P(second red) = 6/14 = 3/7. Multiply: 7/15 × 3/7 = 3/15 = 1/5. (ii) One white and one red can happen in two orders: white then red, or red then white. P(white then red) = (5/15) × (7/14) = 35/210. P(red then white) = (7/15) × (5/14) = 35/210. Total = 70/210 = 1/3. (iii) P(at least one black) = 1 − P(no black). P(no black on first draw) = 12/15 (5 white + 7 red). Given no black on first, P(no black on second) = 11/14 (5 white + 6 red remaining). So P(no black in two draws) = (12/15) × (11/14) = 132/210. Then P(at least one black) = 1 − 132/210 = 78/210 = 13/35.
